prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We study the interaction between two adjacent but electrically isolated quantum point contacts (QPCs). At high enough source-drain bias on one QPC, the drive QPC, we detect a finite electric current in the second, unbiased, detector QPC. The current generated at the detector QPC always flows in the opposite direction than the current of the drive QPC. The generated current is maximal, if the detector QPC is tuned to a transition region between its quantized conductance plateaus and the drive QPC is almost pinched-off. We interpret this counterflow phenomenon in terms of an asymmetric phonon-induced excitation of electrons in the leads of the detector QPC.

outputs.L1: We investigate the interaction between two adjacent yet electrically isolated quantum point contacts (QPCs). When a sufficiently high source–drain bias is applied to one QPC—the drive QPC—we observe a finite electric current in the second, unbiased detector QPC. The current generated in the detector QPC consistently flows in the direction opposite to that of the drive-QPC current. This induced current reaches its maximum when the detector QPC is tuned to a transition region between its quantized conductance plateaus and the drive QPC is nearly pinched off. We interpret this counterflow phenomenon as arising from asymmetric phonon-induced excitation of electrons in the leads of the detector QPC.
outputs.L2: We investigate how two neighboring quantum point contacts (QPCs), which are electrically separated from one another, influence each other. When a sufficiently large source-drain voltage is applied to one of them—the drive QPC—we observe a measurable electric current in the other QPC, which is left unbiased and serves as the detector. This induced current in the detector QPC consistently travels in the direction opposite to the current passing through the drive QPC. The effect is strongest when the detector QPC is adjusted to the transition between quantized conductance plateaus, while the drive QPC is nearly closed off. We explain this counterflow current as resulting from an asymmetric, phonon-mediated excitation of electrons in the detector QPC leads.
outputs.L3:
The study investigates the interaction between two quantum point contacts (QPCs) that are positioned close to one another but remain electrically isolated. This arrangement allows the researchers to examine how current flow through one QPC can influence the behavior of a neighboring QPC without any direct electrical connection between them.

A key observation is that, when a sufficiently large source-drain bias is applied to one of the contacts, referred to as the drive QPC, a finite current appears in the other contact, referred to as the detector QPC, even though the detector QPC itself is not externally biased. This induced current demonstrates that energy or momentum is being transferred from the driven system to the unbiased detector system through an indirect coupling mechanism.

The direction of the induced current is particularly notable. In all cases, the current generated in the detector QPC flows in the direction opposite to the current flowing through the drive QPC. This counterflow behavior distinguishes the effect from simple leakage or conventional current drag and suggests a more subtle mechanism governing the interaction between the two nearby nanostructures.

The magnitude of the induced detector current depends strongly on the conductance states of both quantum point contacts. The effect is most pronounced when the detector QPC is tuned between conductance plateaus, where its transmission is highly sensitive to energy, and when the drive QPC is nearly pinched off. Under these conditions, small energy excitations can produce a relatively large imbalance in transmission through the detector, leading to an enhanced induced current.

The observed counterflow current is interpreted as the result of asymmetric phonon-induced excitation of electrons in the leads of the detector QPC. When the biased drive QPC dissipates energy, it can generate nonequilibrium phonons. These phonons are absorbed by electrons near the detector QPC, exciting them in an asymmetric manner depending on the local electrostatic and transmission properties of the detector. This asymmetry produces a net current through the unbiased detector QPC, with a direction opposite to that of the drive current. Thus, the experiment provides evidence for a nonlocal coupling mechanism between adjacent quantum point contacts mediated by phonon-induced electronic excitations.

The study examines the coupling between two closely spaced but electrically isolated quantum point contacts (QPCs) defined in a two-dimensional electron gas. One QPC is used as a “drive” channel, while the neighboring QPC serves as a “detector.” A large source-drain bias is applied across the drive QPC, forcing it into a strongly nonequilibrium transport regime. At the same time, the detector QPC is kept unbiased, so that any current measured through it cannot arise from a conventional applied voltage but must instead be induced by interaction with the driven system.

The key observation is the appearance of an induced current in the detector QPC when current flows through the drive QPC. Remarkably, this detector current flows in the direction opposite to what would be expected from ordinary momentum drag; it is therefore described as a counterflow current. The induced signal depends sensitively on the conductance settings of both QPCs. It is largest when the detector QPC is tuned between quantized conductance plateaus, where its transmission is strongly energy dependent, and when the drive QPC is close to pinch-off, where transport through the drive channel is highly nonlinear and energetic carriers can be generated efficiently.

These features indicate that the effect is not simply due to direct electrical leakage or capacitive coupling between the two circuits. Instead, the results point to an energy-transfer mechanism. Under high bias, electrons passing through the nearly pinched-off drive QPC can emit nonequilibrium acoustic phonons. These phonons propagate through the host crystal and are absorbed near the detector QPC, where they excite electrons. Because the detector QPC has an asymmetric, energy-dependent transmission probability when tuned between conductance plateaus, phonon-induced electron-hole excitations are transmitted preferentially in one direction. This asymmetry produces a net current even though no external bias is applied to the detector.

The study therefore demonstrates a form of nonlocal interaction between adjacent mesoscopic conductors mediated by nonequilibrium phonons. It shows that a biased QPC can act as a local source of high-energy excitations, while a nearby unbiased QPC can function as an energy-selective detector of those excitations. The observed counterflow current provides evidence that phonon-induced electron excitation, combined with the nonlinear transmission characteristics of a QPC, can generate directed current in an otherwise unbiased nanostructure.
outputs.L5:
QPCs, or quantum point contacts, are narrow constrictions between two wider conducting regions, often created in semiconductor nanostructures. The main purpose of a QPC is to control and study the flow of electrons at extremely small scales, where quantum mechanical effects become important.

A QPC can act like a tunable electronic channel. By applying voltage to nearby gates, researchers can make the channel wider or narrower, allowing more or fewer electrons to pass through. One of the most interesting features of QPCs is conductance quantization, where electrical conductance increases in clear step-like values rather than changing smoothly.

The study of QPCs is important in modern physics and nanotechnology because these devices help scientists understand electron transport, quantum behavior, and low-dimensional systems. A single QPC can also be used as a sensitive detector for nearby electrical charges, making it valuable in experiments involving quantum dots and other nanoscale devices.

In short, QPCs are essential tools for exploring quantum electronics. The QPC remains a simple but powerful structure that continues to support research in advanced semiconductor devices and future quantum technologies.

counterfactuals.output: We report phonon-mediated current drag between two adjacent, electrically isolated quantum point contacts (QPCs). When a finite source–drain bias is applied to a drive QPC, nonequilibrium acoustic phonons emitted by hot carriers propagate to a nearby unbiased detector QPC and generate a dc counterflow current. The detector response is strongly dependent on the QPC transmission and bias polarity, reflecting energy-selective excitation of carriers near one-dimensional subband thresholds. The observed current reverses direction relative to conventional Coulomb drag and is consistent with phonon absorption producing asymmetric carrier populations in the detector constriction. These results demonstrate a nonlocal mechanism for energy transfer and current generation in coupled mesoscopic conductors, highlighting QPCs as sensitive probes of nonequilibrium phonon emission and absorption.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main findings of an experiment on coupled QPCs: one QPC is driven at high source-drain bias, the other is unbiased but shows a current opposite to the drive current, strongest near conductance transitions and drive pinch-off.
counterfactuals.output:
In an experiment with two nearby, capacitively coupled quantum point contacts (QPCs), one QPC was used as a nonequilibrium “drive” channel by applying a large source–drain bias, while the neighboring QPC was left unbiased and monitored for an induced current.

The main findings were:

- **A finite current appeared in the unbiased QPC**, even though no voltage bias was applied to it.
- **The induced current flowed opposite to the current in the driven QPC**, indicating a drag-like effect with negative polarity rather than simple leakage or ordinary positive Coulomb drag.
- **The effect was strongest when either QPC was near a conductance transition**, such as the opening or closing of a 1D subband, where conductance is changing rapidly with gate voltage.
- **The induced current was also enhanced when the driven QPC was near pinch-off**, where transport is highly nonlinear and nonequilibrium fluctuations or energy transfer are strongest.
- The observations suggest that the driven QPC generates nonequilibrium charge or energy fluctuations that are transferred capacitively to the unbiased QPC, producing a rectified current.
- Because the passive QPC has no applied bias, the current likely arises from **interaction-induced drag/rectification**, not direct electrical conduction between the circuits.

Overall, the experiment shows that a strongly biased QPC can drive a counterflow current in a nearby unbiased QPC through Coulomb coupling, with the largest response occurring in regimes where QPC transmission is most energy-dependent and nonlinear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a scientific abstract describing the observation and interpretation of a finite induced current in a detector quantum point contact caused by a neighboring biased but electrically isolated drive QPC.
counterfactuals.output:
We report the observation of a finite dc current through an unbiased detector quantum point contact (QPC) generated by a neighboring, voltage-biased drive QPC that is electrically isolated from the detector circuit. The two QPCs are defined electrostatically in a high-mobility two-dimensional electron gas and coupled only through their local electromagnetic environment and Coulomb interaction. When a source–drain bias is applied across the drive QPC, a measurable current appears in the detector QPC despite zero applied detector bias, demonstrating nonlocal transfer of nonequilibrium energy or momentum between the circuits.

The induced current depends strongly on the conductances of both QPCs and is largest when the detector transmission is energy dependent, particularly near the opening of one-dimensional subbands. Its magnitude increases with drive bias and is sensitive to the drive QPC transmission, consistent with a mechanism governed by nonequilibrium current fluctuations rather than simple leakage. The absence of direct electrical connection, together with the dependence on QPC tuning, rules out trivial circuit cross-talk as the dominant origin.

We interpret the effect as a mesoscopic drag or noise-rectification phenomenon: shot noise and nonequilibrium charge fluctuations produced by the biased drive QPC generate local potential fluctuations in the detector region, which are rectified by the nonlinear, energy-dependent transmission of the detector QPC into a dc current. The sign and magnitude of the induced current are determined by the asymmetry of the detector potential and by the energy dependence of its transmission. These results demonstrate that a biased quantum conductor can drive directed charge motion in a nearby isolated conductor through nonlocal fluctuation-mediated coupling, providing a sensitive probe of nonequilibrium noise, Coulomb interaction, and energy transfer in nanoscale electronic circuits.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal condensed-matter physics language, explain an experiment studying interaction between adjacent quantum point contacts, including the bias conditions, direction of induced detector current, dependence on conductance tuning, and phonon-based mechanism.
counterfactuals.output:
In a typical mesoscopic “QPC–QPC interaction” experiment one defines two laterally adjacent quantum point contacts in the same high-mobility two-dimensional electron gas, separated by a few micrometres or less. One constriction is used as a nonequilibrium emitter or drive QPC, while the second is used as a detector QPC.

A finite source–drain bias \(V_{\mathrm{sd}}^{\mathrm{drive}}\) is applied across the drive QPC, producing a current

\[
I_{\mathrm{drive}} = G_{\mathrm{drive}} V_{\mathrm{sd}}^{\mathrm{drive}},
\]

with \(G_{\mathrm{drive}}\) tuned by its split-gate voltage. The detector QPC is kept at zero applied source–drain bias,

\[
V_{\mathrm{sd}}^{\mathrm{det}} = 0,
\]

so that any measured detector current is not a trivial leakage current but an induced current generated by the nonequilibrium environment produced by the biased drive channel.

Experimentally, when the drive QPC is biased, a finite current appears in the unbiased detector circuit. Its sign is such that the induced detector current flows opposite to the direction of the drive current, i.e. if electrons are driven through the emitter constriction in one direction, the short-circuit current measured through the detector corresponds to carrier motion in the opposite sense. Reversing the polarity of \(V_{\mathrm{sd}}^{\mathrm{drive}}\) reverses the induced response accordingly.

The effect is strongly dependent on the conductance tuning of both QPCs. The detector response is small when the detector QPC is either fully pinched off or tuned onto a flat conductance plateau, where its transmission is nearly energy independent. It becomes largest on the risers between quantized plateaus, especially near

\[
G_{\mathrm{det}} \simeq \frac{1}{2}G_{0},
\qquad 
G_{0}=\frac{2e^{2}}{h},
\]

because there the transmission probability \(T(E)\) has a large energy derivative. In Landauer language, the detector acts as an energy-selective scatterer, so an asymmetric nonequilibrium energy distribution can be rectified into a dc current only when

\[
\frac{\partial T_{\mathrm{det}}}{\partial E} \neq 0.
\]

Similarly, the magnitude of the induced signal depends on the drive-QPC conductance and bias through the dissipated nonequilibrium power. It is enhanced when the drive QPC is partially transmitting or when a new one-dimensional subband is being populated, because electron relaxation and energy emission are then most efficient.

The microscopic coupling mechanism is commonly understood as phonon mediated. Electrons accelerated through the biased drive QPC emerge with excess energy of order \(eV_{\mathrm{sd}}^{\mathrm{drive}}\). They relax in the adjacent two-dimensional electron gas by emitting nonequilibrium acoustic phonons. These phonons propagate through the host crystal and are absorbed in the vicinity of the detector QPC. Absorption creates an asymmetric electronic excitation distribution across the energy-dependent detector barrier. Because the detector transmission is not particle–hole symmetric near a conductance step, this phonon-induced nonequilibrium population is converted into a directed current even though no voltage is applied across the detector.

Thus the experiment demonstrates a nonlocal interaction between neighbouring quantum point contacts: a biased QPC emits nonequilibrium phonons, and an unbiased nearby QPC rectifies the resulting phonon flux into a dc current whose sign is opposite to the drive current and whose magnitude is maximal when the detector conductance is tuned to the steep slopes of its quantized conductance steps.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a short journal-style abstract for a study of counterflow current in an unbiased QPC induced by a nearby high-bias QPC, with maximum response when the detector is between conductance plateaus and the drive QPC is nearly pinched off.
counterfactuals.output: We report measurements of a counterflow current generated in an unbiased quantum point contact (QPC) by a nearby, voltage-biased drive QPC. The induced current flows opposite to the electron flow in the drive circuit and appears only when the detector QPC is tuned to transmit partially. Its magnitude is maximal when the detector conductance lies between quantized plateaus, where transmission is most energy dependent, and when the drive QPC is nearly pinched off under large source–drain bias. These observations indicate that nonequilibrium fluctuations or energy transfer from the biased constriction produce an asymmetric excitation of carriers in the detector. The results demonstrate a sensitive mesoscopic drag-like effect between adjacent QPCs and highlight the role of energy-dependent transmission in converting local nonequilibrium noise into directed current.
